title: The standing prayer
hookLine: the central prayer, said standing, feet together, facing Jerusalem

cards: At one moment in every Jewish service, the room changes. Everyone stands. Feet come together.
People turn, quietly, in the same direction. Lips move, but you hear almost nothing: a murmur, a page turning, someone's shoe. Some sway.
Some stay perfectly still. For several minutes, a room full of people is completely silent and completely busy.
This is the center of every Jewish service, morning, afternoon and evening, and its name just describes what the body is doing.

teach.b: Amidah means standing. The Talmud often just calls it ha-tefillah, the prayer, as if there were no other.

It's also called Shemoneh Esrei, eighteen, for its original eighteen blessings, though the weekday version now has nineteen. Over the coming weeks, they'll come one at a time. The posture is part of the prayer.
Feet together: the Talmud, in Berakhot 10b, connects it to the angels in Ezekiel's vision, where it says "their feet were straight feet." One straight line, as if you had only one leg.
Facing Jerusalem: when King Solomon dedicates the Temple, he asks God to hear people who pray toward their land, toward the city and the house. So in New York, people face east.
In Jerusalem itself, they face the Temple Mount. A blind person, or someone who can't tell direction, the Talmud says, directs their heart instead.

And it's said three times a day. Berakhot 26b gives two explanations: the patriarchs set them, Abraham the morning, Isaac the afternoon, Jacob the evening; or they stand in for the daily offerings of the Temple.

Underneath it all, in the tradition's picture, the one praying is standing before someone. Not lounging, not walking past. Stopping, feet planted, facing one way, and for a few minutes nothing else gets the body.

how: Jews say the Amidah at the morning, afternoon and evening services, standing with feet together and facing toward Jerusalem; it's said silently by each person, and in a congregation with a minyan the leader then repeats it aloud at morning and afternoon services.

games.why: facing Jerusalem is the rule, but someone who can't tell direction directs their heart toward God instead.

practice: If you can, stand up now, feet side by side, hands resting, facing one direction, and notice the small work your body does to stay upright. If you pray, let this be standing before God; if not, standing before the day.
When the minute's up, sit, and keep breathing.
